candidate.answerReason: The longest side must be 3. The remaining two sides sum to 4, giving only the valid sorted triples (1,3,3) and (2,2,3).

methods.label: Bound the longest side and list the possibilities
methods.explanation:
Order the positive integer side lengths as \(a\le b\le c\). Counting in this order avoids counting different arrangements of the same sides. Triangles with the same three side lengths are congruent by SSS.

The triangle inequality requires
\[
c<a+b=7-c,
\]
so \(2c<7\) and hence \(c\le3\). If \(c\le2\), all three sides would be at most \(2\), giving perimeter at most \(6\). Therefore \(c=3\).

The other two sides must sum to \(4\). With \(1\le a\le b\le3\), the only possibilities are \((a,b)=(1,3)\) and \((2,2)\). This gives
\[
(1,3,3)\quad\text{and}\quad(2,2,3).
\]
Both satisfy the strict triangle inequalities, and their different side lengths make them non-congruent. The list is exhaustive, so there are \(\boxed{2}\) triangles, choice \(\mathrm{B}\).
methods.levelReason: The argument uses elementary triangle inequalities, small integer bounds, exhaustive listing, and SSS congruence.

candidate.annotationRationale: Triangle side feasibility is the central target. Congruence properties and SSS justify counting each sorted side triple as exactly one congruence class. The chosen route uses cnm_h003 for the exhaustive finite list, without requiring general integer-equation machinery.

review.mathematicalCheck: For sorted positive integer sides, 2c < 7 gives c ≤ 3, while c ≤ 2 cannot produce perimeter 7. With c = 3, the only remaining pairs are (1,3) and (2,2). Both form triangles, and SSS and congruence properties justify counting exactly two classes.
